Three weeks later and 1 week before admission to this hospital, pain in the left upper quadrant, vaginal bleeding, and headache developed. The patient was admitted to another hospital. The blood level of human chorionic gonadotropin was 24 IU per liter (normal range, <6 IU per liter); the level had been 21,000 IU per liter 3 weeks earlier, when she was pregnant. Blood levels of electrolytes, glucose, amylase, lipase, total protein, and albumin were normal, as were results of renal-function tests, the prothrombin time, the international normalized ratio, and the partial-thromboplastin time. An examination of a peripheral-blood smear for babesia and a direct antiglobulin test were negative; other laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. Imaging studies were obtained. Laboratory Data. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis (Figure 1), performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed splenomegaly (spleen length, 15.6 cm in the craniocaudal dimension; normal range, ≤12 cm), as well as a central filling defect in the splenic vein that was compatible with acute splenic-vein thrombosis. CT of the chest, performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed low lung volumes, scattered ground-glass opacities, and no evidence of pulmonary embolism. CT Scan of the Abdomen.A coronal reconstruction of a CT scan of the abdomen, obtained after the administration of intravenous contrast material, shows splenomegaly (spleen length, 15.6 cm in the craniocaudal dimension), as well as a central filling defect (arrow) in the splenic vein that is compatible with acute splenic-vein thrombosis. Oral contraception was stopped. On the third hospital day, the patient’s abdominal pain diminished, and she was discharged home. Four days later, severe bifrontal headache and loss of vision in the left visual field developed. The patient was evaluated by her primary care physician. On examination, she had decreased peripheral vision superiorly and inferiorly in the left visual field. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was scheduled, but the severity of her headaches increased, and she was evaluated at the other hospital. Additional imaging studies were obtained. CT of the head and neck (Figure 2) revealed a confluent area of hypodensity and sulcal effacement involving the superior right parietal lobe that extended inferiorly into the right occipital lobe and the right aspect of the splenium of the corpus callosum (a finding suggestive of a recent infarct) and small, focal areas of hyperdensity (findings consistent with hemorrhagic conversion). Although a focal occlusive thrombus was not identified, the distal branches of the right posterior cerebral veins were not visible. The patient was transferred to the emergency department of this hospital. Imaging Studies of the Head.A CT scan of the head (Panel A), obtained before the administration of contrast material, shows an area of hypodensity and sulcal effacement involving the right parietal lobe that extends into the right aspect of the splenium of the corpus callosum, a finding suggestive of edema and a recent infarct. Also shown are small, focal areas of hyperdensity, findings consistent with hemorrhagic conversion. A CT venogram (Panel B), obtained in frontal projection after the administration of contrast material, shows no evidence of filling in at least one right cortical vein that drains into the superior sagittal sinus. MRI of the head was performed, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted, and gradient-echo images (Panels C, D, and E, respectively) show evidence of edema, ischemia, and hemorrhage involving the right parietal lobe. A transfemoral cerebral angiogram (Panel F), obtained in lateral projection during the venous phase after the administration of contrast material in the right internal carotid artery, shows multiple filling defects in cerebral veins (arrows), findings that indicate thrombosis of the right frontal and parietal cortical veins, with no involvement of the major dural sinuses. On evaluation in the emergency department, the patient reported persistent headache, vision changes in the left visual field, photophobia, phonophobia, and pain with extraocular movements. She had a history of chronic back pain that was related to a vertebral disk herniation, for which she had undergone spinal-fusion surgery 4 years before admission to this hospital. During the 3 years before admission, she had had two episodes of self-limited thrombocytopenia that were thought to be associated with methotrexate treatment for an unknown skin disorder. She had no history of bleeding or clotting disorders and had had no spontaneous miscarriages. She had a 2-year history of waxing-and-waning dull epigastric pain that was associated with nausea and occasional episodes of bilious emesis; the pain partially improved with omeprazole. The patient’s medications included diclofenac, baclofen, controlled-release morphine sulfate, hydrocodone–acetaminophen, and omeprazole. She had taken oral contraception in the past for extended periods of time. She lived in coastal New England and worked in communications. She drank alcohol occasionally and smoked less than 1 pack of cigarettes per week; she had not smoked during the past few months. She did not use illicit drugs, over-the-counter medications, or herbal medications. There was no family history of bleeding or clotting disorders, spontaneous miscarriage, or hematologic cancer. On examination, the temperature was 38.3°C, the blood pressure 126/72 mm Hg, the pulse 54 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 96% while the patient was breathing ambient air. She was in mild distress because of her headache, but she was alert and oriented to time and place. Examination of the neck, heart, lungs, abdomen, skin, and oral mucosa was normal. Left homonymous hemianopia was present; other cranial-nerve functions were normal, although function of the first cranial nerve was not tested. Strength, sensation to light touch, and deep-tendon reflexes of the arms and legs were normal. Finger–nose–finger testing showed no dysmetria. Examination of a peripheral-blood smear showed 0 to 2 schistocytes per high-power field, teardrop and pencil cells, occasional large platelets, and normal-appearing white cells. Urinalysis showed 1+ ketones, 2+ blood, 1+ protein, 1+ urobilinogen, a specific gravity greater than 1.040 (normal range, 1.001 to 1.035), and a pH of 5 (normal range, 5 to 9) by dipstick; microscopic examination of the sediment revealed no red cells and 3 to 5 white cells per high-power field (normal range, 0 to 2). Other laboratory test results are shown inTable 1. The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit of this hospital, and additional imaging studies were obtained. MRI of the head confirmed the infarcts and hemorrhagic conversion that had been seen on CT angiography and venography (Figure 2). A cortical vein was not visible over the lesion, which suggested either cortical-vein thrombosis or secondary compression due to mass effect of the parenchymal lesion. On the second hospital day, transfemoral cerebral angiography (Figure 2) showed multiple cerebral venous thromboses involving the right frontal and parietal cortical veins, with no involvement of the major dural sinuses. Eleven days later, the patient presented to a second hospital with a new facial droop on the left side, slurred speech, and confusion. The temperature was 36.4°C, the heart rate 102 beats per minute, the blood pressure 141/86 mm Hg, and the oxygen saturation 99% while he was receiving supplemental oxygen through a nasal cannula at a rate of 2 liters per minute. The weight was 63 kg and the BMI 21.9. The patient was oriented to person, place, and time; neurologic examination was notable for a mild facial droop on the left side, mildly increased muscle tone, right foot drop, and symmetric mild weakness in the arms and upper legs. Owing to progressive leukopenia (white-cell count, 1390 per microliter) and thrombocytopenia (platelet count, 51,000 per microliter), methotrexate, clopidogrel, levetiracetam, and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole were discontinued; cyanocobalamin was started. On the fourth hospital day, a fever with a temperature of 38.3°C developed; specimens of blood and urine were obtained for culture, and intravenous vancomycin and cefepime were initiated. The C-reactive protein level was 101.8 mg per liter. Blood tests for ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, influenza type A and B antigens, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) type 1 p24 antigen, antibodies to HIV types 1 and 2, hepatitis B virus surface antigen, hepatitis B virus core antibodies, cytomegalovirus DNA, Epstein–Barr virus DNA, and parvovirus IgM were negative, as were urine tests for legionella antigen and histoplasma antigen. prompt: A 50-year-old obese man (BMI = 32 kg/m2 ) comes to the physician complaining of indigestion after meals, bloating, and heaburn. Vital signs are normal. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this patient.
Let's break down the case step by step.
The patient is a 50-year-old man who's obese with a BMI of 32.
He's complaining about indigestion after meals, bloating, and heartburn.
His vital signs are normal, which is good, but the CT scan shows a hiatal hernia of the esophagus.
The endoscopic biopsy results are a bit detailed, so I need to parse those carefully.
First, the symptoms: indigestion, bloating, and heartburn.
These are classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
Hiatal hernias are often associated with GERD because the hernia can weaken the lower esophageal sphincter, allowing stomach contents to reflux into the esophagus.
So that's a strong clue pointing towards GERD.
Looking at the biopsy findings: thickening of the basal layer of the squamous epithelium.
That makes me think of something causing the esophageal lining to thicken, which is common in chronic inflammation.
The upward extension of the papillae of the lamina propria is another sign of possible inflammation or damage.
The increased number of neutrophils and lymphocytes in the biopsy suggests an inflammatory response, which aligns with GERD because the stomach acid refluxing into the esophagus causes inflammation.
Putting it all together: the patient has symptoms consistent with GERD, a hiatal hernia which is a common cause, and biopsy findings showing esophageal inflammation.
So the most likely diagnosis is gastroesophageal reflux disease.

prompt: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department for shortness of breath. The patient was brought in by paramedics and is currently on 100% O2 via nasal cannula. The patient has a 52 pack-year smoking history and drinks 2 to 3 alcoholic drinks every night. He has a past medical history of asthma but admits to not having seen a physician since high school. His temperature is 98.2В°F (36.8В°C), blood pressure is 157/108 mmHg, pulse is 120/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 77%. Physical exam demonstrates tachycardia with a systolic murmur heard best along the right upper sternal border. Breath sounds are diminished over the right upper lobe. Bilateral lower extremity pitting edema is noted. What best describes the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 65-year-old man who came into the emergency department with shortness of breath.
Let me go through the case step by step.
First, the patient was working on his car with various chemicals and inhalants when he suddenly felt very short of breath.
He didn't get any better with rest, which makes me think it's an acute issue.
He's on 100% O2 via nasal cannula, so his oxygenation isn't great—his saturation is 77%, which is pretty low.
That's a key point because it suggests he's not getting enough oxygen.
Looking at his past medical history, he has a 52 pack-year smoking history, which is significant.
That's a lot of smoking over the years.
He also drinks 2-3 alcoholic drinks every night, so alcohol is part of his lifestyle.
His past medical history includes asthma, but he hasn't seen a physician since high school, so he's probably not managing any chronic conditions, including asthma.
His vital signs are notable for a high pulse rate of 120/min and a high blood pressure of 157/108 mmHg.
His temperature is slightly elevated at 98.2°F, which is within the normal range but could indicate a low-grade fever.
Respirations are 29/min, which is a bit elevated but not critically so.
On physical exam, he has tachycardia, which aligns with his high pulse.
There's a systolic murmur heard best along the right upper sternal border.
That location makes me think of aortic stenosis because the aortic valve is typically heard there.
Systolic murmurs can be innocent or pathological, but given his age and smoking history, it's more concerning for something like aortic stenosis.
His breath sounds are diminished over the right upper lobe.
Diminished breath sounds can be due to atelectasis, pneumonia, or something obstructing airflow.
But considering his asthma history, maybe it's related to that, but he hasn't been treated recently.
Alternatively, it could be due to a pleural effusion or something else compressing the lung.
Bilateral lower extremity pitting edema is present.
That's a sign of fluid overload, which can happen in heart failure.
When the heart doesn't pump effectively, fluid can build up in the legs and sometimes in the lungs, leading to pulmonary edema.
Putting this all together: he's a middle-aged man with a smoking history, presenting with acute breathlessness, low oxygen saturation, tachycardia, a systolic murmur, and peripheral edema.
The murmur along the right upper sternal border points towards aortic stenosis.
Aortic stenosis can lead to left ventricular hypertrophy and eventually left-sided heart failure, which can cause pulmonary edema and dyspnea.
His smoking history increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, which can contribute to aortic stenosis.
His asthma history might be a red herring here because he hasn't been managing it, but the presentation seems more consistent with a cardiac issue.
The combination of the murmur, edema, and acute breathlessness makes me think of aortic stenosis leading to heart failure.
Alternatively, it could be pulmonary embolism, but the physical exam doesn't mention any signs like pleuritic pain or ETOH history that would point more towards that.
Plus, the murmur is more indicative of aortic stenosis.
So, considering all these factors, the most likely diagnosis is aortic stenosis leading to heart failure, causing the symptoms he's presenting with.

prompt: A 23 year old male who is otherwise normal complains of mild pain in his right iliac fossa in a waveform pattern which increases during the night and he becomes exhausted and is admitted in the hospital. The waveform nature of the pain fits with this, as the pain comes in waves as the stone moves.

So, putting it all together: the key findings are hematuria, pyuria (WBCs in urine), and wave-like pain.
This combination is more indicative of a urinary tract infection or possibly a kidney stone causing obstruction and infection.
Since the pain is in the right iliac fossa, it could be related to the right kidney or ureter.
I think the most likely diagnosis is a urinary tract infection, possibly with pyelonephritis, or a kidney stone causing obstruction and infection.
Given the waveform pain and urinalysis, UTI with pyelonephritis seems plausible.
Alternatively, if there's obstruction, it might be a ureteral stone causing colic and infection.

prompt: A 26-year-old man is stabbed in the right intercostal space in the midclavicular line and presents to the emergency department. On examination, subcutaneous emphysema of the right chest wall, absent breath sounds, and a trachea shifted to the left are noted.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this case.
Let's break it down step by step.
The patient is a 26-year-old man who was stabbed in the right intercostal space at the midclavicular line.
That area is on the right side of the chest, a bit below the clavicle.
Stab wounds in this area can be serious because they might puncture the chest cavity.
On examination, the doctor noted subcutaneous emphysema on the right chest wall.
Subcutaneous emphysema means there's air trapped under the skin, which often happens when there's a puncture in the lung or the chest wall.
This air can escape into the tissues, causing swelling and a crackling feeling under the skin.
Next, the patient has absent breath sounds on the right side.
Absent breath sounds usually indicate that the lung isn't inflating properly.
This could be due to a punctured lung (pneumothorax) where air escapes into the pleural space, causing the lung to collapse.
Also, the trachea is shifted to the left.
Normally, the trachea is in the midline, but if there's a pneumothorax on the right, the trachea might shift to the opposite side because the pressure in the right chest is higher, pushing it left.
Putting this all together: a stab wound in the chest, subcutaneous emphysema, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation.
These are classic signs of a pneumothorax.
The stabbing likely caused a tear in the lung or chest wall, allowing air to enter the pleural space.
This leads to the lung collapsing and the symptoms described.
I don't think it's a tension pneumothorax because that usually presents with more severe symptoms like hypotension or shock, which aren't mentioned here.
It's more likely a simple pneumothorax from the stab wound.
The patient's symptoms—subcutaneous emphysema, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation—point to a pneumothorax resulting from the stab wound.

prompt: A 74-year-old man was evaluated in the nephrology clinic of this hospital because of chronic kidney disease. The patient had been in his usual state of health when he was referred to the nephrology clinic of this hospital for a preoperative evaluation of chronic kidney disease, before a transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) for aortic stenosis. Eighteen years before this evaluation, an elevated creatinine level had been found incidentally during an evaluation of fatigue, malaise, and joint stiffness. The patient was evaluated in the nephrology clinic of another hospital, and biopsy of the right kidney was performed. Pathological examination of the kidney-biopsy specimen (Figure 1) revealed glomeruli with thickened capillary walls and mild mesangial hypercellularity. A Jones’ silver stain showed “spikes” and “bubbles” in the glomerular basement membrane, features typical of membranous nephropathy. The interstitium had an infiltrate of mononuclear cells, plasma cells, and eosinophils, with tubulitis and without granulomas or neutrophils. Immunofluorescence showed staining of granular deposits for IgG and C3 along the glomerular basement membrane and in the mesangium. Other stains (C1q, IgA, IgM, fibrinogen, and albumin) were negative. Electron microscopy showed widespread amorphous subepithelial deposits along the glomerular basement membrane and in the mesangium, with surrounding spikes and podocyte foot-process effacement. Arteriosclerosis and glomerulosclerosis were also present. At the other hospital, these findings were interpreted as membranous nephropathy, acute tubulointerstitial nephritis with eosinophils, and arterionephrosclerosis with global glomerulosclerosis. Kidney-Biopsy Specimen.Hematoxylin and eosin staining (Panels A and B) shows glomeruli with thickened capillary walls (Panel A, arrows) and mesangial hypercellularity. There is an interstitial infiltrate of eosinophils (Panel B, arrow) and plasma cells (Panel B, oval). Immunofluorescence (Panel C) shows staining of granular deposits for IgG along the glomerular capillary wall (arrows) and in the mesangium (asterisk). Electron microscopy of a glomerulus (Panel D) shows amorphous subepithelial deposits (arrows) with adjacent spikes in the glomerular basement membrane (arrowheads) and in the mesangium (asterisk); these findings are typical of membranous nephropathy. The patient was told that his kidney disease was consistent with a diagnosis of Sjögren’s syndrome. Prednisone was administered for 6 months and then tapered to a lower dose. Treatment with sodium bicarbonate and furosemide was initiated, as was treatment with losartan, although losartan was intermittently stopped because of hyperkalemia; prednisone was continued. During the next 18 years, the creatinine level gradually increased to 3.28 mg per deciliter (290 μmol per liter; reference range, 0.70 to 1.18 mg per deciliter [62 to 104 μmol per liter]). Twenty-five years before the current evaluation, the patient had received a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis complicated by diabetes mellitus and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. One year later, painless enlargement of the right lacrimal gland occurred. Surgical excision of the right lacrimal gland was performed at the other hospital, and examination of the excised specimen reportedly revealed nonspecific inflammation. The next year, enlargement of the left lacrimal gland and the bilateral submandibular and parotid glands developed. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck, performed before and after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed masslike abnormalities of the bilateral submandibular and parotid glands. The abnormalities were hypointense on T1-weighted and T2-weighted imaging. The patient declined another glandular biopsy and was told that he probably had Sjögren’s syndrome. Glandular enlargement resolved, and during the next 23 years, the patient was treated with prednisone for presumptive Sjögren’s syndrome. Two years before the current evaluation, shortness of breath and substernal chest pressure on exertion developed; these symptoms usually resolved after approximately 20 minutes of rest. The patient was evaluated at the other hospital, and aortic stenosis was diagnosed. Four months before the current evaluation, the shortness of breath and substernal chest pressure worsened, such that the patient became unable to carry his groceries a short distance to his house. Additional imaging and cardiology studies were obtained. Computed tomography (CT) of the heart, chest, abdomen, and pelvis, performed before and after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed multiple large aneurysms involving all the coronary arteries, with associated mural thrombus (Figure 2A through 2D; andVideo 1, available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org). There was extensive coronary-artery calcification, along with scattered pulmonary nodules measuring up to 4 mm in diameter, multiple mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes, and calcification in the tail of the pancreas. Cardiac CT Scans and Coronary Angiography.Curved, multiplanar, reformatted CT images of the left anterior descending artery (Panel A), left circumflex artery (Panel B), and right coronary artery (Panel C) show aneurysms involving all the coronary arteries, with mural thrombus (white asterisks) adjacent to contrast-enhanced coronary arteries (white arrowheads). There is extensive coronary-artery calcification. A three-dimensional volume-rendered CT image of the heart (Panel D) shows aneurysms involving the left main artery (black arrowhead), left anterior descending artery (white arrowhead), left circumflex artery (white arrow), and right coronary artery (black arrow), with the contrast-enhanced lumen depicted in red and adjacent mural thrombus depicted in yellow. The complete blood count and blood levels of electrolytes, vitamin B12, folic acid, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, glucose, total protein, albumin, globulin, and thyrotropin were normal, as were results of liver-function tests. Screening tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus antibodies and p24 antigen were nonreactive. An electrocardiogram was normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest was performed to assess the status of the patient’s known, treated lung cancer. Changes attributed to a lobectomy of the right lower lobe and a segmentectomy of the posterior right upper lobe for a lung cancer were noted, with no new findings or findings that were suspicious for recurrent lung cancer. However, a rim-enhancing mass was noted at the 11 o’clock position in the right breast; this mass was new since the previous chest CT scan obtained 16 months earlier (Figure 1A). Mammography and ultrasonography were recommended as follow-up diagnostic procedures. This mass was new since the previous chest CT scans (not shown). A mammogram of the right breast was obtained 2 days after discharge. The craniocaudal view (Panel B) and the mediolateral–oblique view (Panel C) show a spiculated mass with architectural distortion that corresponded to the mass on the chest CT scan and was new since the previous mammogram, which had been obtained 2 years earlier (craniocaudal view, Panel D; mediolateral–oblique view, Panel E). prompt: An 18 year old male presents to OPD with pain in lower right tooth region with no remarkable medical history. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 18-year-old male who presented with pain in his lower right tooth.

Next, the radiographic examination is key here.
It mentions a well-defined multilocular radiolucency with scalloping around the root of tooth 43.

A radiolucency means there's a area where the X-ray image appears darker, indicating less dense tissue, like a cavity or a cyst.

Scalloping around the root is another important clue.

Putting this together, the most likely diagnosis is a dentigerous cyst.
Dentigerous cysts are the most common type of odontogenic cysts and typically occur around the crown of a tooth, often near the roots.
They can cause expansion of the jawbone and scalloping of the adjacent roots.
Since the patient is 18, it's a typical age for such cysts to present, as they can develop during the formation of the roots of the teeth.

I don't think it's a simple cyst like a radicular cyst because those are usually associated with a specific tooth's root and might not present as multilocular.

So, considering all these factors—age, radiographic appearance, and clinical presentation—the diagnosis is likely a dentigerous cyst.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this patient.

I know that the Philadelphia chromosome is a specific abnormality seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), where a part of chromosome 22 fuses with chromosome 9, leading to the BCR-ABL gene.
Since it's absent, that rules out CML.
So, considering the elevated platelets with abnormalities, I'm thinking of a myeloproliferative disorder.
The two main possibilities are essential thrombocythemia (ET) and chronic myeloid leukemia.

I don't think it's another condition like polycythemia vera because that usually involves all three cell lines (red cells, white cells, platelets) being elevated, and the platelet abnormalities aren't as specific.
Also, the absence of the Philadelphia chromosome makes me more confident it's not CML.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is essential thrombocythemia.

The patient's symptoms, including shortness of breath, nonproductive cough, fine crackles, and clubbing, along with his history of chemotherapy for testicular cancer, suggest bleomycin-induced interstitial lung disease.

I'm thinking about possible conditions that affect attention and behavior in children.
ADHD comes to mind because it's characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity.

ADHD often presents in academic settings where the child can't stay focused, leading to poor performance despite having average intelligence.

I don't see any signs of other conditions like learning disabilities because his reading is fine, and his IQ is normal.

prompt: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for a routine physical exam. The patient is concerned about his performance in school and fears he may fail out. He recently did poorly on an exam and it has caused him significant stress. He also is worried that his girlfriend is going to leave him. The patient claims that he thought he was going to be an incredible doctor some day, but now he feels like a terrible person. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the most likely diagnosis for this 26-year-old man based on the case presentation.
Let me go through the information step by step.
First, the patient is concerned about a burning sensation in his throat after eating large meals.
He's worried about esophageal cancer because his uncle had it.
That's a red flag, but I need to consider other possibilities too.
He has a past medical history of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and constipation.
His medications include whey protein, fish oil, multivitamin, and sodium docusate.
He's stressed about school performance, fearing he might fail out, and is anxious about his girlfriend leaving him.
He feels like he's a terrible person, which is a significant emotional burden.
He also mentions guilt over his grandfather's death a year ago and reexperiences the funeral.
He takes melatonin for trouble sleeping and prays every four hours, hoping things will improve.
Putting this together, the burning sensation in the throat could be related to something like gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), which can cause heartburn.
However, the patient's symptoms are more psychological.
He's overwhelmed with stress, anxiety, and guilt, which are strong indicators of a possible mental health issue.
His constant worrying, feelings of guilt, reexperiencing a traumatic event (the funeral), and sleep disturbances point towards an anxiety disorder.
Specifically, generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) seems likely because he's anxious about multiple areas of his life—school, relationships, his health, and his grandfather's death.
The persistent worry and stress are central to GAD.
While I considered GERD initially, the psychological symptoms are more prominent and likely the primary issue.
His stress and anxiety could be exacerbating the throat burning, but the main diagnosis here is probably an anxiety disorder.

prompt: A 43-year-old woman has had a 10-year history of severe and recurrent peptic ulcer disease (PUD) that is refractory to medical therapy. She has had ulcers at multiple sites of the small bowel including the distal duodenum and jejunum.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 43-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe and recurrent peptic ulcer disease (PUD) that's not responding to medical therapy.
She's had ulcers in multiple sites of the small bowel, including the distal duodenum and jejunum.
First, I know that PUD typically refers to ulcers in the stomach or the duodenum, usually caused by Helicobacter pylori or NSAID use.
But this patient has ulcers in the jejunum as well, which is less common.
That makes me think it's not just a standard PUD case.
I remember that some conditions cause ulcers in the small intestine.
One possibility is Crohn's disease, which is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Crohn's can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, including the jejunum.
It's chronic and can be refractory to standard PUD treatments because it's not caused by acid or H. pylori.
Another thought is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES).
This condition causes excessive production of stomach acid due to gastrin-secreting tumors in the pancreas or duodenum.
It can lead to multiple ulcers, including in the small intestine, and the ulcers are often resistant to conventional therapy because of the high acid levels.
I should consider the presentation.
ZES typically presents with multiple ulcers, especially in the jejunum and duodenum, and can cause complications like bleeding or perforation.
It's also associated with symptoms like diarrhea and abdominal pain.
Since her ulcers are refractory, ZES is a strong possibility.
Crohn's disease, on the other hand, is more associated with other symptoms like weight loss, fever, and anemia, and it can cause strictures or fistulas.
While it can cause ulcers, the presentation here seems more aligned with ZES because of the multiple refractory ulcers in the small bowel.
I should also think about other causes like intestinal tuberculosis or ischemic bowel disease, but those are less common and usually present with different symptoms.
Intestinal TB would likely have more systemic symptoms and positive结核 tests, which aren't mentioned.
Ischemic bowel is more common in older adults with risk factors like atherosclerosis, which isn't specified here.
So, putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
The patient's history of multiple, refractory ulcers in the small bowel fits this condition well.
The patient's history of multiple, refractory ulcers in the small bowel, particularly the jejunum and distal duodenum, suggests Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES).
ZES is characterized by excessive gastrin production due to tumors, leading to increased stomach acid and ulcers that are resistant to standard PUD treatments.

prompt: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the hospital with increasing shoness of breath and dry cough for the past few years. He smokes 1.5 packs of cigarettes and drinks about four bottles of beer a day. He is constantly "gasping for air" and now walks with difficulty because he becomes breathless after only a few steps. Prolonged expiration with wheezing is noted. Physical examination shows a barrel chest, hyperresonance on percussion and clubbing of the digits. The patient's face is puffy and red, and he has pitting edema of the legs. A chest X-ray discloses hyperinflation, flattening of the diaphragm and increased retrosternal air space.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 55-year-old man.
Let's break down the case presentation step by step.
First, the patient has a history of increasing shortness of breath and a dry cough for a few years.
He's a heavy smoker, smoking 1.5 packs a day, and drinks a lot of beer.
His main symptoms are difficulty breathing, needing to gasp for air, and trouble walking because he gets breathless after just a few steps.
On physical exam, he has a barrel chest, which makes me think of something related to chronic lung issues.
Hyperresonance on percussion suggests hyperinflation of the lungs, which is common in conditions like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Clubbing of the digits is another clue; that's often seen in chronic hypoxia, which can occur in COPD or other lung diseases.
He also has a puffy, red face and pitting edema in his legs.
Pitting edema usually indicates fluid overload, which can happen in right-sided heart failure.
The face being puffy and red might be due to polycythemia, which can occur in chronic hypoxia as the body tries to compensate by increasing red blood cell production.
Looking at the chest X-ray findings: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, and increased retrosternal air space.
These are classic signs of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, specifically emphysema.
The hyperinflation leads to a barrel-shaped chest, and the diaphragm appears flattened because the lungs are hyperinflated, pushing the diaphragm down.
Putting it all together, the patient's symptoms, physical exam findings, and imaging all point towards COPD.
His smoking history is a major risk factor, and the progression of symptoms over years aligns with the chronic nature of the disease.
The edema could be a result of right ventricular failure secondary to chronic hypoxia from COPD, leading to pulmonary hypertension.
So, considering all these factors, the most likely diagnosis is Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, specifically emphysema.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 75-year-old man who's been having trouble reading for the past year.

The fundoscopic exam showed localized retinal elevation and drusen.
I remember that drusen are those yellow deposits under the retina, right?
They're often associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
The Amsler grid test is something patients use to check for distortions or blind spots, which can be a sign of AMD.
Fluorescein angiography results showed early hyperfluorescence.
From what I recall, in AMD, especially the wet form, you get abnormal blood vessels that leak dye, causing hyperfluorescence.
Early hyperfluorescence might indicate the presence of these new vessels or leakage.
Putting it all together: localized retinal elevation suggests something is bulging, which could be due to a subretinal neovascular network in wet AMD.
The drusen are classic for AMD.
The Amsler grid findings would likely show metamorphopsia or missing areas, which align with AMD symptoms.
The fluorescein showing hyperfluorescence supports the idea of choroidal neovascularization, which is a key feature of wet AMD.

The patient's symptoms, fundoscopic findings of drusen and localized retinal elevation, along with fluorescein angiography showing early hyperfluorescence, point towards age-related macular degeneration, particularly the wet form, due to the presence of choroidal neovascularization.

prompt: A 34-year-old man is referred for evaluation of hypeension and persistent hypokalemia in spite of taking oral potassium supplements. Blood pressure is 180/110 mm Hg. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L (normal 140 to 148 mEq/L); potassium, 3.3 mEq/L (normal 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L); Bicarbonate, 29 mEq/L (normal 22 to 29 mEq/L); Chloride, 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 107 mEq/L); and Urea nitrogen, 23 mg/dL (normal 7 to 18 mg/ dL). Computed tomography demonstrates a 3-cm mass in the right adrenal gland.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 34-year-old man with hypertension and hypokalemia despite taking potassium supplements.
Let's break down the information step by step.
First, his blood pressure is really high at 180/110 mm
Hg.
That's definitely in the stage 2 hypertension range.
Now, looking at his lab results: sodium is slightly elevated at 149 mEq/L, which is just above the normal range.
His potassium is low at 3.3 mEq/L, which is definitely hypokalemia.
Bicarbonate is on the higher end at 29 mEq/L, but that's still within normal limits.
Chloride is normal, and urea nitrogen is elevated at 23 mg/dL, which is a bit concerning.
The CT scan shows a 3-cm mass in the right adrenal gland.
That's a big clue.
Adrenal masses can be either adenomas or something more serious like pheochromocytoma or even metastasis, but given the age and presentation, primary aldosteronism comes to mind.
Primary aldosteronism is a condition where the adrenal glands produce too much aldosterone.
This leads to sodium retention and potassium loss, which explains the hypokalemia and high sodium levels.
The hypertension is also a classic symptom because aldosterone causes vasoconstriction and increased blood volume.

In this case, the patient's hypokalemia isn't responding to oral supplements, which is typical in aldosterone-secreting tumors because the excess aldosterone promotes potassium excretion regardless of intake.
The elevated urea might be due to the body's response to high blood pressure, possibly from aldosterone's effects on blood volume and kidney function.
So putting it all together: a mass in the adrenal gland, hypokalemia, high sodium, and resistant hypertension point towards an aldosterone-producing adenoma, which is a form of primary aldosteronism.

prompt: A 10 years old male patient came with complaint of headache and vomiting for past 20 days. On examination, patient has an ataxic gait. NCCT revealed a fouh ventricular mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus. CE-MRI was done to characterize the lesion .

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 10-year-old boy.
He's been having a headache and vomiting for 20 days, and when he was examined, he had an ataxic gait.
The NCCT showed a fourth ventricular mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus, and they did a CE-MRI to characterize the lesion.
Alright, let's break this down.
First, the symptoms: headaches and vomiting for over three weeks.
That's a long time, so it's not something minor like a stomach bug.
The ataxic gait means his walking is unsteady, which often points to issues with the cerebellum or the brainstem, maybe.
The fourth ventricle is part of the brain's ventricular system, and masses there can block the flow of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to hydrocephalus.
So, the imaging shows a mass in the fourth ventricle causing obstruction.
The CE-MRI would help determine what kind of lesion it is—like whether it's a tumor, an infection, or something else.
Since it's causing hydrocephalus, it's obstructing the flow of CSF, which can increase intracranial pressure.
Now, thinking about possible lesions in the fourth ventricle.
Common ones include tumors like ependymomas, which are glial cell tumors arising from the ependyma lining the ventricles.
They can obstruct CSF flow.
Another possibility is a choroid plexus papilloma, which can also cause hydrocephalus.
Infections like abscesses or inflammatory conditions could be another cause, but the presentation here is more chronic, so maybe less likely.
Alternatively, it could be a dermoid cyst or other developmental cysts, but those usually don't cause obstruction unless they're large.
Ependymomas are more common in children and can occur in the fourth ventricle.
They can cause hydrocephalus by blocking the flow of CSF from the fourth ventricle into the spinal canal.
The symptoms of increased intracranial pressure like headaches and vomiting align with this.
The ataxia could be due to the mass effect on the cerebellum or brainstem.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is an ependymoma in the fourth ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
The patient presents with a chronic history of headaches and vomiting, along with an ataxic gait.
Imaging reveals a fourth ventricular mass causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
Given the location and the symptoms, the most likely diagnosis is an ependymoma, a tumor commonly found in the fourth ventricle that obstructs CSF flow and leads to hydrocephalus.

prompt: A 26 year old man complains of abdominal distension, swelling of the legs and easy fatigability. His blood pressure is 90/70 mm Hg and pulse becomes difficult to feel on inspiration. JVP is grossly elevated and rises further on deep inspiration. He has pedal edema, ascites and tender hepatomegaly. Precordium is quiter with loud and some what early apical third heart sound.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 26-year-old man with various symptoms.
Let's break down the case presentation step by step.
First, the patient complains of abdominal distension, which makes me think of possible fluid buildup, maybe ascites.
He also has swelling in his legs, so edema is present.
Easy fatigability could be due to heart or kidney issues.
His blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg, which is a bit low, but not critically so.
The pulse being difficult to feel on inspiration makes me think of pulsus paradoxus, which is a sign of constrictive pericarditis or other conditions that restrict heart filling.
The jugular venous pressure (JVP) is grossly elevated and rises further on deep inspiration.
That's a classic sign of constrictive pericarditis because the pericardium restricts the heart's ability to expand, so venous pressure increases, especially when the patient inspires deeply.
He has pedal edema, which is fluid retention in the legs, and ascites, which is fluid in the abdomen.
Both are signs of fluid overload, often due to heart or kidney failure.
The tender hepatomegaly suggests the liver is enlarged, possibly due to venous congestion, which can happen in right-sided heart failure.
In the precordium, the heart sounds are quite, with a loud and somewhat early apical third heart sound.
An early S3 is often a sign of heart failure, as the heart is trying to compensate by ejecting more blood, leading to an extra sound during early diastole.

Putting this all together: the combination of low blood pressure, elevated JVP that increases on inspiration, ascites, edema, hepatomegaly, and an early S3 heart sound points towards constrictive pericarditis.
This condition causes the pericardium to become rigid, preventing the heart from expanding properly, leading to elevated venous pressures and fluid accumulation in the abdomen and legs.
The heart's compensatory mechanisms might explain the early S3 sound.
I don't think it's heart failure because the JVP elevation is more pronounced in constrictive pericarditis.
Also, the patient's age is quite young, making pericarditis more likely than typical heart failure.
Other possibilities like cirrhosis are less likely because the JVP is elevated, which isn't usually seen in liver cirrhosis without heart involvement.
So, the most likely diagnosis is constrictive pericarditis.
The patient presents with symptoms indicative of fluid overload and signs of constrictive pericarditis.
The elevated JVP, especially increasing on inspiration, along with ascites, edema, and an early S3 heart sound, strongly suggest this condition.
Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by a rigid pericardium that restricts heart expansion, leading to venous congestion and fluid retention.

To help manage his symptoms, the patient adjusted his diet from solid food to soft solid food. Although the patient had not eaten food for 24 hours before the procedure, the stomach could not be adequately visualized because there was a large amount of residual food; no intraluminal masses were seen. prompt: A 32-year-old man was admitted to this hospital after 2 weeks of confusion and headache and 2 days of fever. The patient had been in his usual state of health until 1 month before admission, when his wife noted that he began to have behavior suggestive of anxiety. Two weeks before admission, his wife noted that he began to have confusion; for example, he was unable to recall the ages of his children or to correctly identify the date. At that time, headache and neck stiffness developed. Two days before admission, fever developed. On the day of admission, the patient had worsening confusion and somnolence, and his wife brought him to the emergency department of this hospital for evaluation. On presentation, the patient was not able to provide any history but was accompanied by his wife, who described his recent symptoms. His medical record showed a 10-year history of Behçet’s disease, which had initially been complicated by oral and genital ulcers and intermittent fever. During the following decade, flares of Behçet’s disease had been associated with various manifestations: pulmonary embolism, iliac artery aneurysm and dissection, bilateral renal vein thrombosis, erythema nodosum, deep venous thrombosis, uveitis, an inferior vena cava clot complicated by superior vena cava syndrome that led to thrombectomy, and renal infarction. The flares of Behçet’s disease had usually included oral ulcers, genital ulcers, uveitis, or fever. Past treatment for Behçet’s disease had included azathioprine, cyclosporine, and prednisone. Two years before this presentation, treatment with azathioprine and cyclosporine was discontinued and adalimumab initiated. Attempts to taper the dose of prednisone resulted in flares of genital and oral ulcers. The frequency of adalimumab administration was increased to weekly, but genital and oral ulcers persisted. Thirteen months before this presentation, treatment with adalimumab was stopped and infliximab initiated. Diffuse arthralgias developed that were attributed to infliximab. Twelve months before this presentation, treatment with infliximab was stopped and golimumab initiated. But given the liver enzymes, it's more likely related to liver disease.
Tender hepatomegaly and ascites point towards something like cirrhosis or acute liver failure.
But the patient recently delivered a normal baby, so maybe something related to pregnancy?
Could it be acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP)?
That's a condition where there's rapid onset of jaundice, liver dysfunction, and often ascites in pregnant women.

prompt: A 20 year old woman presents with hemoptysis, bilateral conductive deafness and palpable purpura on the legs. X ray chest shows a thin walled cavity in left lower zone. Investigations shows a leukocyte count of 12000/mm3, red cell casts in the urine and serum creatinine 3mg/dL.

She also has palpable purpura on her legs, which are purple spots that can be felt, indicating some kind of bleeding under the skin, possibly from a clotting issue or platelet problem.
Looking at the imaging, a chest X-ray shows a thin-walled cavity in the left lower zone.

Putting this together, the key points are hemoptysis, deafness, purpura, and kidney involvement.
The purpura could be due to a vasculitis, which is an inflammation of blood vessels.
Vasculitis can present with various symptoms, including skin lesions, respiratory issues, and kidney problems.
One possibility that comes to mind is Goodpasture syndrome.
It's a rare condition where there's an autoimmune issue causing glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage.
The symptoms would include hemoptysis because of the lung involvement, and the kidney issues align with the lab findings.
The deafness might be due to some involvement of the middle ear, possibly from the vasculitis affecting those vessels.
Another thought is Wegener's granulomatosis, but that usually presents with more systemic symptoms like sinusitis or uveitis, and the deafness might be more related to sinus involvement.
However, the presence of both kidney and lung issues is more in line with Goodpasture.
Alternatively, maybe it's a form of Henoch-Schönlein purpura, which is a type of vasculitis that can affect multiple systems, including the kidneys and lungs.
But HSP typically presents with abdominal pain and arthritis as well, which aren't mentioned here.

The thin-walled cavity in the lung on X-ray could be a result of the underlying vasculitis causing some sort of infarction or abscess, but in Goodpasture, it's more about pulmonary hemorrhage leading to cavitation.
The elevated white count supports infection or inflammation, and the red cell casts in the urine are classic for glomerulonephritis, which is a hallmark of Goodpasture.
So, considering all these factors—hemoptysis, kidney issues, purpura, and the imaging findings—the most likely diagnosis is Goodpasture syndrome.
The patient presents with hemoptysis, bilateral conductive deafness, palpable purpura, and a thin-walled cavity on chest X-ray.

Suprasellar masses are typically located near the pituitary gland, which is in the center of the brain.

prompt: A 70-year-old women presents to her primary care physician with sudden episodes of dizziness that resolve in certain positions. On further questioning she describes a false sense of motion with occasional spinning sensation consistent with vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses or hearing loss aside from presbycusis. Her vital signs are normal. During the physical exam the the patient reports an episode of vertigo after transitioning from sitting to supine and horizontal nystagmus is concurrently noted. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 70-year-old woman who's having these episodes of dizziness and vertigo.
Let me start by breaking down the information given.
First, she presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that go away when she's in certain positions.
That makes me think of something positional, maybe related to the inner ear or the balance system.
She mentions a false sense of motion and a spinning sensation, which is classic for vertigo.
Vertigo is different from regular dizziness because it's that intense feeling of movement, often spinning.
She doesn't have any recent illnesses, and her hearing loss is only from presbycusis, which is age-related.
So, no sudden hearing loss, which rules out something like Meniere's disease, I think.

Her vital signs are normal, so no signs of systemic issues like low blood pressure or something neurological.
During the physical exam, she had an episode of vertigo when she moved from sitting to supine.
That position change is key.
Also, horizontal nystagmus was noted.
Nystagmus is an eye movement that's often a sign of a vestibular issue.
So, putting this together: vertigo triggered by position changes, nystagmus, and her age.
This sounds a lot like Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).
BPPV is common in older adults and is caused by tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear moving incorrectly, which send false signals to the brain about the body's movement.
The nystagmus also aligns with BPPV because the eyes move in a specific pattern when the vestibular system is off.
I don't think it's something like a stroke because her symptoms are positional and not sudden onset with other neurological signs.
Migraines can cause vertigo, but they usually come with headaches and aren't necessarily positional.
Labyrinthitis is another possibility, but that's often accompanied by hearing loss and is more acute.
So, considering all this, BPPV seems like the most likely diagnosis.
The patient's symptoms of vertigo triggered by positional changes, along with horizontal nystagmus, strongly suggest Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).
BPPV is a common condition in older adults where tiny calcium crystals in the inner ear dislodge and cause false movement signals.
The absence of hearing loss other than presbycusis and the lack of systemic symptoms support this diagnosis over other possibilities like Meniere's disease or stroke.

prompt: Lalloo, 50 years old, a chronic smoker, presents with history of hemoptysis. He was having truncal obesity and hypeension. He had an elevated ACTH level which was not suppressible with high dose dexamethasone.

ACTH is produced by the pituitary gland and stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol.

One possibility is a pituitary tumor that's secreting ACTH (like a pituitary adenoma), but that's less likely here because the patient has other symptoms pointing towards a lung issue.
Another possibility is an ectopic ACTH secretion.
This happens when a tumor outside the pituitary gland, often in the lungs, produces ACTH.
This is commonly associated with small cell lung cancer, which can secrete various hormones, including ACTH.
This condition is known as ectopic ACTH syndrome.
Given that the patient is a smoker, has a history of hemoptysis, and an elevated ACTH level that doesn't suppress, it points towards small cell lung cancer.

So, considering all this, the most likely diagnosis is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

prompt: A 38-year-old man presents to the physician with fever and malaise for 4 days. He has headaches and joint pain. A pruritic rash appeared on the trunk yesterday. He had blood in his ejaculate twice. His hearing has become partially impaired. There is no history of serious illnesses or the use of medications. Ten days ago, he traveled to Brazil where he spent most of the time outdoors in the evenings. He did not use any control measures for mosquito bites. His temperature is 38.2в„ѓ (100.8в„‰); the pulse is 88/min; the respiratory rate is 13/min, and the blood pressure is 125/60 mm Hg. Conjunctival suffusion is noted. A maculopapular rash is present over the trunk and proximal extremities without the involvement of the palms or soles. Several joints of the hands are tender to palpation. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. A peripheral blood smear shows no pathogenic organisms. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this patient.
Let's go through the case step by step.
The patient is a 38-year-old man with a 4-day history of fever and malaise.
He also has headaches, joint pain, and a pruritic (itchy) rash on his trunk that appeared yesterday.

Additionally, he experienced blood in his ejaculate twice, partial hearing impairment, and he traveled to Brazil 10 days ago, spending a lot of time outdoors in the evenings without using mosquito control measures.
His vital signs show a temperature of 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse 88/min, respiratory rate 13/min, and blood pressure 125/60 mm
Hg.
On exam, he has conjunctival suffusion, a maculopapular rash on the trunk and proximal extremities (but not palms or soles), tender joints in the hands, a soft abdomen without organomegaly.
The peripheral blood smear didn't show any pathogenic organisms.
First, I'm thinking about the travel history.
Brazil is a country where several mosquito-borne diseases are prevalent, like dengue, Zika, and Chikungunya.
The fact that he was outdoors in the evenings and didn't use protection makes me think of these possibilities.
The symptoms include fever, malaise, headache, joint pain, rash, and conjunctival suffusion.
These are classic for dengue fever.
The rash is maculopapular and doesn't involve the palms or soles, which is typical for dengue.
The joint pain is more in the hands, which is common in dengue but can also occur in other arboviral diseases.
The blood in the ejaculate and hearing impairment are concerning.
Dengue can sometimes cause hemorrhagic manifestations, like petechiae or even more severe bleeding, but blood in the ejaculate is less common.
However, it's possible if there's some mucosal bleeding.
Hearing impairment is more commonly associated with Zika virus, but it can also occur in dengue in some cases.
The blood smear didn't show any organisms, which might rule out some bacterial infections, but it's not specific for viral ones.
Dengue is a viral infection, so the smear wouldn't show the virus itself unless there's a secondary infection.
Another possibility is Chikungunya, which also causes fever, rash, and joint pain.
However, Chikungunya typically causes more severe joint pain, especially in the small joints of the hands and feet, and the rash is usually more fleeting.
The hearing impairment is less common with Chikungunya.
Zika virus can cause similar symptoms, including fever, rash, and joint pain, but it's more associated with neurological symptoms like Guillain-Barré syndrome and, in this case, hearing impairment.
However, the rash in Zika is usually more widespread and can include the palms and soles, which isn't the case here.

The absence of organomegaly and no signs of meningitis or encephalitis on exam makes me think less of other viral hemorrhagic fevers like yellow fever or West Nile, which can have more severe neurological or liver involvement.
Putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is dengue fever.
The symptoms, travel history, and exam findings align well with this.
The hearing impairment and blood in the ejaculate could be due to the systemic effects of the virus causing some mucosal bleeding and temporary auditory issues.

The patient's symptoms, including fever, rash, joint pain, and travel history to Brazil, along with the absence of pathogenic organisms in the blood smear, point towards dengue fever as the most likely diagnosis.
The conjunctival suffusion and maculopapular rash are consistent with dengue, and while hearing impairment and blood in the ejaculate are less common, they can occur due to systemic effects.

prompt: About 12 days after a mild upper respiratory infection, a 12-year-old boy complains of weakness in his lower extremities. Over several days, the weakness progresses to include his trunk. On physical examination, he has the weakness described and no lower extremity deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, or pain. Spinal fluid studies are notable for elevated protein only.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 12-year-old boy.
Let's break down the case step by step.
First, the patient had a mild upper respiratory infection about 12 days ago.
Now, he's complaining of weakness in his lower extremities, which has progressed to include his trunk.
On exam, he has weakness, no deep tendon reflexes, no muscle atrophy, and no pain.
The spinal fluid studies show elevated protein only.
Hmm, so the key points here are the progression of weakness from lower extremities to the trunk, absence of reflexes, and elevated protein in the spinal fluid.
I remember that weakness in the lower extremities that ascends could be a sign of a neurological issue, maybe something affecting the nerves or the spinal cord.
The absence of deep tendon reflexes suggests a problem with the lower motor neurons or peripheral nerves.
The elevated protein in the spinal fluid makes me think of conditions that cause an immune response, like an infection or inflammation in the central nervous system.
But he had a URI recently, which might be a clue.
Could it be a post-viral condition?
Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) comes to mind.
GBS typically presents a few days to weeks after an infection, often a respiratory or gastrointestinal one.
It's an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system attacks the peripheral nerves, leading to muscle weakness, areflexia, and sometimes ascending paralysis.
The progression of weakness from legs to trunk fits GBS.

The elevated protein in the CSF is also a hallmark, as it's due to the immune response causing increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier, allowing proteins like immunoglobulins to enter the spinal fluid.
Other possibilities to consider: acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), which is essentially the same as GBS.
Maybe also consider multiple sclerosis, but that usually has other symptoms like optic neuritis or brain lesions, which aren't mentioned here.
Poliomyelitis is another thought, but it's usually caused by a virus and would have more systemic symptoms, and the CSF would show more cells than just elevated protein.
So putting it all together, the most likely diagnosis is Guillain-Barré syndrome.

The patient's symptoms of ascending weakness, areflexia, and elevated spinal fluid protein, following a URI, strongly suggest Guillain-Barré syndrome, an autoimmune response causing peripheral nerve inflammation.

prompt: A 9-month-old girl is brought in by her father for a scheduled check-up with her pediatrician. He states that over the past 4-5 months she has had multiple ear infections. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 9-month-old girl.

She's had multiple ear infections over the past 4-5 months and was hospitalized for an upper respiratory infection two months ago.

Her medical history includes eczema and allergic rhinitis, which are both allergic conditions.

Given that her IgA and IgM are normal, it's less likely to be something like X-linked agammaglobulinemia or severe combined immunodeficiency, which would affect multiple immunoglobulins.
Since the family history doesn't mention immunodeficiencies, it's probably a primary rather than secondary issue.
So, putting it all together, the low IgG with normal others and recurrent infections points towards common variable immunodeficiency.
The patient presents with multiple ear infections, a history of eczema and allergic rhinitis, and low IgG levels with normal IgA, IgE, and IgM.
These findings are consistent with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), a primary immunodeficiency characterized by low IgG and possible low IgA levels, leading to recurrent infections.

prompt: A 68-year-old man was admitted to this hospital because of worsening confusion. The patient had a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease. An axial diffusion-weighted image from MRI (Panel E) shows multiple new foci of acute infarction involving the left thalamus, the left lentiform nucleus, and the right frontal white matter (arrows). On the fourth hospital day, the patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility with plans for an oncology evaluation after discharge. After 10 days at the rehabilitation center, he was discharged home. Three days after discharge from the rehabilitation center, and 1 week before the current admission, numbness and tingling in the right hand and forearm developed, and the patient’s daughter again took the patient to the other hospital. On examination, he had pronator drift of the right arm and dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing. MRI of the head revealed new foci of acute infarction involving the left thalamus, the subcortical white matter of the right frontal lobe, and the periventricular white matter on the left side, but there was no hemorrhage. Treatment with apixaban was stopped, and enoxaparin was started. The patient was discharged home on the third hospital day. Five days after discharge, the patient’s daughter noticed that the patient had new difficulty with swallowing pills and worsening confusion, and she brought him to the emergency department of this hospital for evaluation. The patient was not able to provide additional history, but his daughter reported that his aphasia and difficulty with balance had worsened since discharge from the other hospital. Other medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and obesity. Medications included enoxaparin, aspirin, atorvastatin, and metformin. There were no known drug allergies. The patient lived alone in a suburb of Boston and was retired. He had smoked cigarettes for 40 years, but he had recently decreased tobacco use from one pack per day to three cigarettes per day. He smoked marijuana occasionally, and he drank alcohol rarely. His father had had coronary artery disease with a myocardial infarction in the fourth decade of life. The temporal temperature was 36.6°C, the blood pressure 158/75 mm Hg, the pulse 70 beats per minute, the respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and the oxygen saturation 98% while the patient was breathing ambient air. The body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) was 25.1. The patient was alert and interactive. He was able to answer orientation questions correctly, although he was slow to respond. His speech was fluent, with no paraphasic errors. He had some difficulty with following simple commands and was unable to follow complex commands. There was decreased activation of the right nasolabial fold with preserved wrinkling of the forehead. Pronator drift of the right arm was present, and there was mild hemiparesis on the right side. The remainder of the examination was normal. Blood levels of electrolytes and rheumatoid factor were normal, as were results of liver-function and kidney-function tests. prompt: A 14-year-old girl was admitted to this hospital because of swelling of the left jaw. The lesion was easily separated from the thin, expanded cortical margins. The inferior alveolar nerve (arrow) was preserved. The high vascularity of the tumor imparts a red-brown appearance to the lesion that is typical of brown tumors and other giant-cell–rich lesions (Panel B). Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the initial maxillary tumor–biopsy specimen before excision (Panel C) shows a nodule of the brown tumor that is partially surrounded by trabeculae of reactive bone. sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 17-year-old girl who hasn't started her period yet.

That's a bit concerning.

The pelvic exam shows a blind vaginal pouch.
A blind pouch usually means that the vagina is present but doesn't lead to the cervix, which could indicate a problem with the development of the reproductive tract.
Also, the ultrasound didn't show a uterus or ovaries.
That's a big clue.
If the uterus and ovaries aren't visualized, it suggests that they might be absent or malformed.
Putting this together, the absence of the uterus and ovaries on ultrasound points towards a congenital anomaly.
One possibility is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome.

Also, the inguinal mass could be a hernia, but combined with the pelvic findings, it's more likely related to the reproductive system.
So, considering all these factors—delayed menarche, blind vaginal pouch, no uterus or ovaries on ultrasound—the most likely diagnosis is Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome.

prompt: A 23-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for knee pain. The pain started yesterday and has not improved since then. The patient is generally in good health. She attends college and plays soccer for her school's team. Three days ago, she was slide tackled during a game and her leg was struck from the outside. She fell to the ground and sat out for the rest of the game. It was not until yesterday that she noticed swelling in her knee. She also feels as if her knee is unstable and does not feel confident bearing weight on her leg during athletic activities. Her past medical history is notable for asthma, which is currently treated with an albuterol inhaler. On physical exam, you note bruising over her leg, knee, and lateral thigh, and edema of her knee. Passive range of motion of the knee is notable only for minor clicking and catching of the joint. The patient's gait appears normal, though the patient states that her injured knee does not feel stable. Further physical exam is performed and imaging is ordered. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 23-year-old woman who came in with knee pain.
Let me start by going through the case presentation step by step.
First, the patient is a college student who plays soccer.

She fell and sat out the rest of the game.
Initially, she didn't notice any swelling until yesterday, and now she's experiencing pain that hasn't gone away.
She also mentions that her knee feels unstable and she's not confident putting weight on it during activities.
Her past medical history includes asthma, which is treated with an albuterol inhaler, but that's probably not directly related here.
On physical exam, there's bruising on her leg, knee, and lateral thigh, along with edema (swelling) of the knee.
Passive range of motion shows minor clicking and catching, but her gait is normal.
However, she feels her knee isn't stable.
So, thinking about possible injuries from a soccer tackle.
Slide tackles can often lead to injuries like ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) tears, especially if the knee is struck from the outside.
The fact that she felt a pop or something during the tackle is a common symptom of an ACL tear.
The delayed swelling might be due to the initial impact not causing immediate severe damage, but the ligament tear leading to internal bleeding and swelling over time.
The clicking and catching during passive range of motion are also indicative of a ligament injury.
ACL tears often cause instability because the ligament provides crucial support to the knee joint.
Even though her gait is normal, the instability she feels is significant.
Other possibilities to consider: a meniscus injury, but that usually presents with more localized pain and might not cause as much instability.
A sprained ligament (like a MCL or LCL tear) could also be a possibility, but the mechanism of injury and symptoms lean more towards an ACL tear.
The fact that she was struck from the outside makes ACL more likely because that's a common direction for such tears.
Imaging, like an MRI, would confirm the diagnosis, but based on the history and physical exam findings, ACL tear is the most likely diagnosis.

The patient's history of a slide tackle causing a lateral blow to the knee, followed by delayed swelling and instability, along with physical exam findings of bruising, edema, and joint instability, strongly suggest an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear.

prompt: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 40 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital in active labor. The patient reports severe pelvic pain. Pregnancy has been complicated by gestational diabetes. Pregnancy and delivery of her first child were uncomplicated. Current medications include insulin, folic acid, and a multivitamin. Vital signs are within normal limits. The cervix is 100% effaced and 10 cm dilated; the vertex is at -1 station. The fetal heart rate is reactive with no decelerations. Epidural anesthesia is performed and the patient's symptoms improve. Ten minutes later, the patient has dizziness. Her pulse is 68/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is begun. What is the most likely underlying cause of the patient's hypotension?

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the most likely diagnosis for this case.
Let's break it down step by step.
The patient is a 27-year-old woman who's 40 weeks pregnant, so she's full term.
She's in active labor and reports severe pelvic pain.
Her obstetric history is significant for gestational diabetes, but her first delivery was uncomplicated.
She's on insulin, folic acid, and a multivitamin.
Vital signs are normal, which is good.
The cervix is 100% effaced and 10 cm dilated, which means she's fully dilated.
The vertex is at -1 station, so the baby's head is just beginning to appear at the vaginal opening.
The fetal heart rate is reactive with no decelerations, which is a good sign for the baby's well-being.
She received epidural anesthesia, and her symptoms improved, which makes sense because epidurals relieve pain.
But then, ten minutes later, she developed dizziness.
Her vital signs showed a pulse of 68, respirations 16, and blood pressure 90/60.
That's low blood pressure, or hypotension.
They started IV fluids, which is a common treatment for hypotension.

So, the question is: what's causing her hypotension after the epidural?

Epidurals can cause hypotension because they block sympathetic nerve impulses, leading to vasodilation.
This can reduce systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.
It's a common side effect, especially in the early stages of labor.
The patient's symptoms improved with the epidural, but then she developed dizziness, which is a sign of hypotension.
Other possibilities to consider: Could it be something else like a blood loss?
But she's fully dilated and the vertex is at -1 station, so it's not like she's delivering yet.
There's no mention of bleeding or other signs like a drop in hemoglobin.
Also, she's receiving IV fluids, which would help if it was a volume issue.
Another thought: Could it be aortocaval compression?
That's when the uterus compresses the vena cava, reducing venous return and causing hypotension.
But that usually happens in the later stages, especially when the uterus is large, which it is here.
However, aortocaval compression typically causes more of a transient hypotension and might present with other symptoms like nausea or vomiting, which aren't mentioned here.
But wait, she just had an epidural.
Epidurals can cause a significant drop in blood pressure due to vasodilation.
The timing makes sense—right after the epidural, she developed dizziness.
So it's likely the epidural-induced hypotension.
I don't think it's sepsis or an allergic reaction because there's no fever, rash, or other signs.
Also, the blood pressure wasn't extremely low; it was 90/60, which is manageable with fluids.
So putting it all together, the most likely cause is epidural anesthesia-induced hypotension.
The patient experienced hypotension after receiving epidural anesthesia, which is a known side effect due to vasodilation and reduced systemic vascular resistance.
This is the most likely cause given the timing and context.

sentences.s: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out the diagnosis for this 22-year-old man who presented with pain and rapidly spreading erythema on his left hand.

He suddenly developed pain and swelling in his left hand, specifically involving the distal interphalangeal joint of the second finger and the proximal interphalangeal joint of the fourth finger.
Over several hours, bullae formed, which turned dark purple.
He also had spreading erythema on his hand, forearm, and upper arm into the axilla.
No other symptoms like fatigue, dyspnea, or pain elsewhere.
On examination, he had violaceous, tender bullae on the dorsal aspect of his left hand.
The erythema was nontender and spreading.
His vital signs showed a slightly elevated temperature (38.6°C) and tachycardia (101 bpm).
Blood tests showed leukocytosis with a high neutrophil count, which suggests a bacterial infection.
Other labs were mostly normal, except for slightly elevated liver enzymes and a prolonged prothrombin time, which might indicate some inflammation or coagulation issues.
Imaging with CT showed soft-tissue swelling over the affected joints but no signs of bone erosion, fractures, or fluid collections.
That makes me think it's not an infection involving bone or joint spaces like septic arthritis, but rather something in the soft tissues.
The patient's history of recent activity is crucial.
He recently started taxidermy, handling a frozen deer hide.
He scraped the skin and fur, removing ticks, and then massaged a mixture of deer brain and water into the hide.
He didn't wear gloves or protective clothing.
His mother helped but remained well.
This makes me think of zoonotic infections.
Handling animal hides, especially deer, can expose him to various pathogens.
The rapid progression of symptoms, bullae, and erythema suggest a severe reaction, possibly an infection.
One possibility is an infection caused by the bacteria Francisella tularensis, which causes tularemia.
Tularemia can present with skin lesions, including ulcers and bullae, and is often associated with handling animals or their products.
The incubation period is about 3-5 days, which fits with his symptoms starting four days after handling the hide.
Another consideration is anthrax, but that typically presents with black eschars and is more associated with handling hides of infected animals, especially in areas where anthrax is endemic.
However, the bullae and the spread of erythema are more suggestive of tularemia.
The patient was treated with IV fluids, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin.
While these are broad-spectrum antibiotics, tularemia is typically treated with aminoglycosides or fluoroquinolones.

Putting it all together: the patient's history of handling a deer hide, the rapid onset of bullae and erythema, leukocytosis, and the imaging findings pointing to soft-tissue infection all point towards tularemia.

No dyspnea, fever, or pleuritic chest pain.
